stem: A fictional cafe in Gaborone employed 40 people at the start of the year and 50 at the end. Nine employees left during the year.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the cafe's labour turnover, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain one way in which this level of labour turnover could affect the cafe.

points.description: Leavers must be replaced, so recruitment and training costs rise
Application: the cafe must advertise for and train new staff each year
New staff are less experienced, so service may be slower and customers may be lost

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Each of the nine leavers must be replaced, so the cafe pays for advertising, selection and training. New staff are less experienced, so service may be slower and customers may be lost.

explanation: Turnover 20.0%; replacement costs and lower service quality.
hints: Use the average number of employees.

stem: A fictional clothing factory in Lusaka pays its sewing machinists a piece rate.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Define the term 'piece rate'.

points.description: A method of payment based on the number of units produced
Earnings rise with output, at a fixed rate per unit

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A piece rate is a method of payment in which an employee is paid a fixed amount for each unit produced, so earnings rise with output.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain one disadvantage to the factory of paying a piece rate.

points.description: Workers may hurry to produce more units
Application: garments may be badly sewn or cloth spoiled
The factory may need extra inspection, adding cost, or may lose customers

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Machinists may hurry to produce more garments, so garments may be badly sewn or cloth spoiled. The factory may then need extra inspection, which adds cost, or lose customers who receive faulty goods.

hints: Think about the effect on quality.

stem:
Sunrise Call Centre is a fictional business in Johannesburg. It handles customer calls for banks. In Year 2 it opened a second floor and recruited 45 new agents, giving each only one day of induction and no further training. Hourly pay was not changed. Agents say that supervisors never ask for their ideas, that targets are very high and that the new floor is noisy and poorly ventilated. The managing director believes that the business should "pay more and the staff will stay".

|  | Year 1 | Year 2 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Employees at start of year | 58 | 66 |
| Employees at end of year | 66 | 84 |
| Employees who left | 11 | 27 |
| Hourly pay (US\$) | 4.50 | 4.50 |
| Customer complaints per month | 12 | 29 |

Labour turnover = employees leaving ÷ average number of employees × 100. Labour retention = 100 − labour turnover.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: Teaching an employee the skills for the present job is called {{blank:a}}, while introducing a new employee to the business is {{blank:b}}.

parts.explanation: Training is for the present job; induction introduces new staff.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: For Year 2, calculate (to one decimal place):

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the labour turnover;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the labour retention.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain two possible reasons why employees have left Sunrise Call Centre.

points.description: Little induction and no training, so agents may feel unable to cope
Application: new agents had one day of induction
Poor working conditions, noise and poor ventilation
Application: the new floor is noisy and poorly ventilated, which causes stress and ill health

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: New agents had only one day of induction and no further training, so many may have felt unable to cope with the job. The new floor is noisy and poorly ventilated, which causes stress and ill health and makes agents look for work elsewhere.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Analyse the effects of the rise in labour turnover on Sunrise Call Centre.

points.description: Recruitment, selection and training costs rise
Application: 27 leavers had to be replaced in Year 2
New agents are less experienced and make more errors
Application: complaints rose from 12 to 29 a month
Complaints may lead banks to cancel contracts, reducing revenue

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The 27 leavers had to be replaced, so recruitment, selection and training costs rose. New agents are less experienced and make more errors, and complaints rose from 12 to 29 a month. If the banks cancel contracts because of the complaints, the call centre's revenue will fall.

parts.explanation: Cost and quality chain with data.
hints: Costs first, then quality, then revenue.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Assess two non-financial methods that Sunrise Call Centre could use to motivate its agents.

points.description: Employee participation, such as a suggestion scheme or regular meetings
Benefit: agents would feel listened to and could suggest ways to reduce stress from targets
Limit: managers must act on the suggestions or motivation falls
Training and development for agents
Benefit: trained agents would handle calls better and see a future
Limit: training costs money and trained agents may leave for rivals

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Participation, such as a suggestion scheme or monthly meetings, would make agents feel listened to and could produce ideas to reduce the stress from high targets, but managers must act on the ideas or motivation will fall. Training and development would help agents to handle calls better and see a future, but it costs money, and trained agents may leave for rivals.

hints: Give a benefit and a limit for each method.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: The managing director believes that the business should "pay more and the staff will stay". Evaluate this view and advise Sunrise Call Centre on how to reduce labour turnover.

points.description: Pay was not changed, and low pay may be one reason agents leave
Herzberg: pay is a hygiene factor; higher pay may reduce dissatisfaction but not solve other problems
Agents' complaints are about induction, ideas, targets and the working environment, which pay does not solve
A pay rise increases costs for all agents, whether or not they would have left
Non-financial changes (induction, training, participation, ventilation) may cost less and address the causes
Retention is 64.0%, so the cost of replacing leavers is large and justifies some spending
Advice with a reason and time-frame, for example improve induction and conditions first and review pay in six months

levels.descriptor: Weighs pay against the other causes in the case using the data; reaches a justified recommendation with a time-frame
Explains pay and other causes with some use of the case; judgement weakly supported
States causes or remedies with little evaluation

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Pay has not changed and low pay may be one reason agents leave. Herzberg argued that pay is a hygiene factor, so a rise may reduce dissatisfaction but would not by itself motivate. The agents' complaints, however, are about a one-day induction, no training, no say in decisions, high targets and a noisy, poorly ventilated floor, and a pay rise for everyone would not remove these causes and would raise costs for agents who would have stayed anyway. Non-financial changes such as a longer induction, training, a suggestion scheme and improved ventilation may cost less and tackle the causes directly. Because only 64.0% of agents stay, replacing leavers is costly, so some spending is justified. The managing director should improve induction and conditions first and review pay in six months in the light of turnover and complaints.

parts.explanation: Weighs pay against other causes and gives time-framed advice.
hints: Compare what pay can and cannot fix with what the agents complain about.

explanation: Turnover 36.0%, retention 64.0%; poor induction and conditions drive leaving; pay alone is not the answer.
hints: Use the average of the start and end numbers.
Link each cause to the data.

stem: Essay. A fictional hotel in Livingstone has labour turnover of 35%, much higher than the average for hotels in the area. The owner is considering a large investment in staff training.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Analyse two benefits to the hotel of training its staff. [8 marks]

points.description: Training improves skills, so service and quality improve
Application: better-trained receptionists and waiters satisfy guests
Better service attracts repeat bookings and raises revenue
Training shows that the hotel values its staff, raising motivation
Motivated staff are less likely to leave, reducing labour turnover
Application: fewer leavers means lower recruitment and induction costs
Multi-skilled staff can cover absences
Application: the hotel needs fewer temporary staff in busy periods

levels.descriptor: Two benefits analysed with developed chains and application to the hotel
Two benefits explained with some application
Benefits stated with little development

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Training improves skills, so receptionists and waiters serve guests better, which brings repeat bookings and more revenue. Training also shows that the hotel values its staff, raising motivation, and motivated staff are less likely to leave, so labour turnover and the costs of recruiting and inducting replacements fall. A further benefit is that multi-skilled staff can cover absences, so the hotel needs fewer temporary staff in busy periods.

parts.explanation: Two benefits with chains of analysis.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether training is the best way for the hotel to reduce its labour turnover. [12 marks]

points.description: Training can raise skills, motivation and the feeling of a future
It is costly in fees and in lost output while staff learn
Application: with 35% turnover, many trained staff would leave, so the money may be wasted
Turnover may be caused by low pay, long hours or poor management, which training does not solve
Pay or conditions may address the causes more directly
A survey of leavers would show the real causes
Non-financial methods such as participation or job rotation may cost less
Trained staff may be poached by rivals
Training should be linked to promotion or pay so that staff stay
Success depends on the cause of turnover and the cost compared with the savings
Judgement: training alone is unlikely to be best
Reasoned conclusion with a condition or time-frame

levels.descriptor: Balanced evaluation of training against other methods, using the causes of turnover and cost; a justified conclusion with a condition
Explains training and at least one alternative with some application; judgement weakly supported
Describes training with little evaluation

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Training can raise skills and motivation and give staff a sense of a future, which may keep them. But it is costly in fees and in lost output while staff learn, and with turnover as high as 35% many trained staff may leave, so the money could be wasted. Turnover may also be caused by low pay, long hours or poor management, which training does not address, and trained staff are at risk of being poached by rivals. The hotel should first survey leavers to find the real causes. Pay, conditions or non-financial methods such as participation and job rotation may be cheaper and more direct. Training is therefore unlikely to be the best way on its own; it is worthwhile if the survey shows that lack of skills and prospects are the causes, and if it is linked to promotion or pay so that trained staff have a reason to stay.

parts.explanation: Weighs training against the causes of turnover and alternatives.

explanation: Training benefits; training alone is unlikely to be the best answer without knowing the causes.

stem: Essay. A fictional bank in Harare plans to move most of its services online and close half of its branches over two years. Many staff fear for their jobs and branch managers are opposed.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Analyse two ways in which the bank could reduce resistance to this strategic change. [8 marks]

points.description: Explain the reasons for the change early
Application: show staff how online banking protects the bank's future and their jobs
Honest communication reduces fear of the unknown
Involve staff in planning the change
Application: branch managers could help to design which branches close
Involvement gives a sense of ownership and reduces opposition
Train and redeploy staff
Application: branch cashiers could be trained for online support, reducing fear of job loss

levels.descriptor: Two ways analysed with developed chains and application to the bank
Two ways explained with some application
Ways stated with little development

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The bank could explain the reasons for the change early and honestly, showing staff how online banking protects the bank's future and their jobs, which reduces fear of the unknown. It could also involve staff, such as branch managers, in planning which branches close, which gives them a sense of ownership and reduces opposition. Training cashiers for online support would also reduce fear of job loss.

parts.explanation: Two ways with chains of analysis.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether the success of the bank's strategy depends mainly on its corporate culture. [12 marks]

points.description: Corporate culture is the shared values and ways of working
A role culture, common in banks, favours rules and may be slow to adopt change
Application: branch managers used to authority may resist the change
A culture that supports innovation makes the change easier
Other factors matter: the quality of the strategic analysis and choice
Application: customers' willingness to use online banking, security and competitors
Leadership matters; a transformational leader could inspire staff
Resources and timing matter: money, technology and the two-year plan
Culture can be changed, but slowly
Culture and strategy must fit; a good strategy fails if implementation fails
Judgement: culture is important but not the only factor
Reasoned conclusion with a condition or time-frame

levels.descriptor: Balanced evaluation of culture against other factors using the case; a justified conclusion with a condition
Explains culture and at least one other factor with some application; judgement weakly supported
Describes culture with little evaluation

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Corporate culture matters because strategy has to be carried out by people. A bank is likely to have a role culture, based on rules and procedures, which is careful but slow to accept change, and branch managers used to authority may resist closing branches. A culture that values innovation would make the change easier. But other factors also decide success: the strategic analysis, such as whether customers are willing to use online banking and how secure it is; competitors' moves; the quality of leadership, since a transformational leader could inspire staff; and resources and timing, since two years may be too short. Culture can be changed, but only slowly. Culture is therefore important, but not the only factor. The strategy is most likely to succeed if the bank is realistic about its role culture, builds support through involvement, and allows enough time.

parts.explanation: Weighs culture against analysis, leadership and resources.

explanation: Reduce resistance by communication, involvement and training; culture is important but not the only factor.
hints: Use communication, involvement and training for (a).
Compare culture with at least two other factors in (b).

stem: A fictional dental practice in Mutare can open a second clinic at a cost of US\$23,000. The owner estimates a 0.58 chance of strong demand, when the clinic would bring in US\$64,000, and a 0.42 chance of weak demand, when it would bring in US\$27,000 (before the cost of the clinic). If she does nothing, there is no extra income or cost.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the expected value of the new clinic;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the net expected value of the new clinic.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Analyse one limitation of using the net expected value to decide whether to open the clinic.

points.description: The probabilities are estimates by the owner
Application: if strong demand is only a 0.45 chance, the net expected value falls
The result is an average, not what will happen once
Application: if demand is weak the clinic gains only 4,000 after its cost, so the owner might prefer to avoid the risk

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The probabilities are the owner's estimates, so if strong demand is really less likely than 0.58 the net expected value falls. It is also an average, not what will happen once: if demand is weak the clinic gains only US\$4,000 after its cost, so a cautious owner might prefer to avoid the risk.

parts.explanation: One limitation, analysed with the figures.

explanation: EV US\$48,460; net US\$25,460; probabilities are estimates and EV is an average.
hints: Net expected value = expected value − cost.

stem: A fictional supermarket chain in Gaborone plans to introduce self-service tills. Managers score the forces from 1 (weak) to 5 (strong). Driving forces: cost saving 4, customer demand 5, faster queues 3. Restraining forces: staff fear of job loss 5, cost of equipment 4, customers' lack of confidence 4. After a programme of staff consultation, training and a customer helper at each till, the restraining scores become 3, 4 and 2.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the balance (driving total minus restraining total):

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: before the programme;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: after the programme.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Analyse why the programme changes the balance of forces.

points.description: Consultation and training reduce staff fear of job loss
Application: the score for staff fear falls from 5 to 3
A customer helper increases customers' confidence
Application: the score for customers' lack of confidence falls from 4 to 2
Reducing restraints is usually more effective than raising pressure, because pressure can increase resistance

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Consultation and training reduce staff fear of job loss, so that score falls from 5 to 3. A customer helper at each till increases customers' confidence, so that score falls from 4 to 2. Reducing restraints is usually more effective than adding pressure, because more pressure can increase resistance.

parts.explanation: Links each action to a restraining force.

explanation: Balance −1 before and +3 after; actions reduce restraints.

stem: Msasa Logistics is a fictional company in Harare with a role culture and a corporate plan to double its fleet in five years. It must choose between Option X, a new depot (cost US\$46,000), and Option Y, leasing space (cost US\$19,000). The managers estimate a 0.72 chance that demand grows and a 0.28 chance that it does not. Option X brings in US\$104,000 if demand grows and US\$28,000 if not; Option Y brings in US\$58,000 if demand grows and US\$33,000 if not (before cost). Drivers and depot staff fear that a new depot will change their jobs, and the owner is concerned that rivals may respond with price cuts.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the net expected value of:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Option X;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Option Y.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Analyse how the company's role culture might affect the implementation of the chosen option.

points.description: A role culture follows rules and procedures
Application: staff may stick to existing routes and resist a new depot
Decisions pass through several levels, so implementation may be slow
Application: the plan to double the fleet in five years may need faster decisions

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A role culture follows rules and procedures, so drivers and depot staff may stick to existing routes and resist a new depot. Decisions pass through several levels, so implementation may be slow, which could make it hard to meet a plan to double the fleet in five years.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Evaluate which option the company should choose.

points.description: Option X has the higher net expected value (US\$36,720 against US\$32,000), a difference of US\$4,720
Option X costs US\$27,000 more and its worst case is lower: 28,000 − 46,000 = a loss of US\$18,000, against a gain of US\$14,000 for Y
The 0.72 probability is an estimate and the ranking could change
A new depot fits the five-year plan to double the fleet but staff resistance and rival price cuts add risk
Resources and attitude to risk: the owner's concern about rivals suggests caution
Judgement with a reason and condition

levels.descriptor: Uses both net values and worst cases, the plan, culture and rival response; a justified recommendation with a condition
Applies some figures and case facts with some analysis; judgement weakly supported
States figures or options with little analysis

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Option X has the higher net expected value, US\$36,720 against US\$32,000, but it costs US\$27,000 more and its worst case is a loss of US\$18,000 (28,000 − 46,000), whereas Option Y still gains US\$14,000 (33,000 − 19,000). The probability of 0.72 is an estimate, so the ranking could change. A depot fits the five-year plan to double the fleet, but staff resistance in a role culture and the risk of rival price cuts add risk. Given the owner's concern about rivals, Y is the safer start, with X to follow if demand growth is confirmed and staff have been consulted.

parts.explanation: Weighs return against risk using the case and recommends Y first with a condition.
hints: Compare return and worst case, then bring in the plan, culture and rivals.

explanation: X US\$36,720; Y US\$32,000; X returns more but Y is safer.
hints: Net expected value = expected value − cost.

stem: Zambezi Courier is a fictional delivery company in Lusaka. To cut costs it moved all 200 drivers from full-time contracts to zero-hours contracts and now uses an app that tracks each driver's speed and ranks drivers by ratings. Costs per parcel fell by 18% in the first year, but driver turnover rose to 70%, customer complaints doubled and two large clients have said that they may leave. The managing director plans to continue and add more monitoring. The company's corporate culture has become one of tight control. Evaluate whether the managing director should continue with this approach to HRM.

points.description: Zero-hours contracts match labour to demand and lower fixed costs
Application: costs per parcel fell 18%
The approach is hard HRM, treating drivers as a cost to be controlled
Monitoring gives control of speed and ratings
Application: the app lets the company rank drivers
Turnover of 70% raises recruitment and training costs
Complaints doubled and clients may leave, threatening revenue
Insecure drivers lose commitment, so service quality falls
A softer approach (minimum hours, training, a say in the app's rules) may improve retention
The company's culture of tight control may resist a change of approach
Strategic change needs communication and involvement to reduce resistance
Judgement with a reason and condition, for example move part-way to a softer approach for the best drivers

levels.descriptor: Balanced evaluation of hard HRM using the data, culture and the risk to clients; considers a softer approach and the difficulty of change; a justified conclusion with a condition
Analyses costs and problems with application; some evaluation; judgement supported
Explains benefits or problems with some application; limited judgement
Describes the approach with little application

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The hard approach has worked in one way: zero-hours contracts match labour to demand, and costs per parcel fell by 18%, while the app gives the company control over speed and ratings. But the costs are growing. Driver turnover of 70% means constant recruitment and training, insecure drivers have less commitment, and customer complaints have doubled. Two large clients have said they may leave, which would threaten revenue and could outweigh the cost savings. Adding more monitoring may increase stress and turnover further. A softer approach, with minimum guaranteed hours, training and a say in the app's rules, might keep the best drivers and improve service, although it would raise costs and reduce flexibility. Changing would not be easy, as a culture of tight control is likely to resist, so the managing director would need to communicate the reasons and involve managers and drivers. He should not simply continue: he should move part-way to a softer approach for the best drivers, keep flexibility for the rest, and review turnover, complaints and client retention after six months.

explanation: Hard HRM cut costs but harmed service and retention; a partial move towards a softer approach is advised.
hints: Weigh the 18% saving against turnover, complaints and the clients at risk.
